scene1.text: …Why is it so loud this early in the morning…
Thud. Thud. Thud.
Father: 'Gregor? Gregor, what's the matter?'
He hasn't left for work yet? That's strange.
Grete: 'Gregor? Are you alright? Are you feeling ill?'
Gregor: 'I'm fine.'

choices.label: Ask him to open his door

scene1.text: He doesn't sound fine. And he's still not out the door. This isn't good.
Grete: 'Gregor, please open the door. Please.'
Silence.

choices.label: Get dressed and go to the living room

scene1.text: Suddenly, a few knocks at the front door.
A man from the office. He walks straight past us toward Gregor's door as if he already owns the answer.
Manager: 'Mr. Samsa. Open the door, please. The company requires an explanation for your absence.'
Gregor: 'I can't.'
Why won't he open it? What is he hiding?
Gregor is the only reason this family stays afloat. If he loses this job —
What happens to us then?
Hiss. Hiss. Hiss.
Manager: 'That — that sounds like an insect.'
Mother: 'Oh God. He must be terribly ill — Grete, go, quickly — fetch a doctor, now!'

choices.label: Rush out and find a doctor

scene1.text: Grete: 'Yes — yes, I'm going!'
Huh...huh...huh..
Grete: The doctor is here!
No one responds.
Mother sits motionless in her chair, her face soaked with tears, while Father sits nearby, his head lowered, as if weighed down by something he cannot bear to face.
Grete: Father, where's the manager? Is Gregor okay?
Father remained silent, stealing a weary, helpless glance toward Gregor's room from the corner of his eye.

scene2.text: It has been a month since my brother turned into a huge insect.
Our lives have changed completely since then.
I started to take care of Gregor.
To keep the family afloat, father has returned to work
But that wasn't enough to make up for the loss
So I had to work for  money  too.
Every day became a long day after that.
I have to be careful not to lose my  sanity  due to exhaustion.
Oh poor brother, when will you be back?

violinScene.text: We were reaching our limits
Father: 'There is no other way. We need the income.'
We had no choice but to rent out one of our room to three lodgers
We gave them the best room in the apartment.
Of course we did
Things has been rather stable since then, until one day
It was the lodgers who asked me to play.
I should have said no.
For a few bars it seemed possible that the music might hold the room together.
Then I heard it.
That sound from the hallway.
That familiar dragging weight against the floorboards.
I didn't stop playing. I told myself I didn't hear it.
Then the lodgers rose from their chairs.
He was in the doorway.
He came out for the music. I knew it the moment I saw him.
Something in him heard the violin and moved toward it the way he always used to.
Back when he was the one who paid for my lessons.
Back when he used to ask me to play on Sunday evenings — anything, it doesn't matter what.
The lodgers left that night. All three of them.
I am twenty years old.
I have a job and calluses on my fingers and I come home each evening already emptied out.
Father is furious...
Mother hasn't spoken.
I stand there in the wreckage of the evening, I feel something in my chest go very quiet.
I understand that I have reached the end of something...
Grete: We have to get rid of it. I won't use his name.
She said it.
The words came out steadier than she expected.
Mother made a sound. Father looked at the floor.
Neither of them disagreed.
In the morning, he was gone.
The charwoman found him first. She called it matter-of-factly, the way you report a broken pipe or a dead houseplant.
Grete stood in the hallway and listened to her parents cry and felt something she could not name.
Not grief. Not relief. Something in between that had no word.
She thought about the conservatory on Brünn Street.
She had not thought about it in months.
She noticed, distantly, that she felt like herself again.
Outside, it was spring.
THE END
